result.summary: Pausanias lists further statues of Olympic victors at Olympia, noting their sculptors and some stories about the athletes. He doubts the tale of Damarchus turning into a wolf, and tells of Timanthes' self-immolation and Timasitheus' death after joining Isagoras at Athens.

scenes.title: Statues of early victors
scenes.summary: Pausanias names victors and sculptors, including Amertus, Euanoridas, Damarchus and Eubotas. He rejects the wolf-transformation tale about Damarchus.

scenes.title: Timanthes and Arcadian athletes
scenes.summary: Statues of Timanthes, Baucis and Arcadian athletes are listed. Timanthes is said to have burned himself alive when he could no longer bend his bow.
scenes.stakes: Timanthes cannot bear losing his strength and chooses death.

scenes.title: Timasitheus of Delphi
scenes.summary: Timasitheus won many victories and was brave in war. He joined Isagoras' seizure of the Acropolis and was executed by the Athenians.
scenes.stakes: Timasitheus risks his life by joining Isagoras' attempt to seize Athens.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias' judgment that such self-destruction is madness rather than bravery.

analysis.text: Pausanias weighs athletic fame against folklore, skeptically judging tales like the wolf-man and the self-burning athlete.
Olympic statues served as public records of victories, and Pausanias uses them as evidence, including for the Isagoras episode in Athenian politics around 508 BC.

legacy.text: The Damarchus wolf story belongs to the Arcadian werewolf tradition, often cited in the history of lycanthropy legends.

fun_facts.text: Euanoridas is said to have compiled a list of Olympic victors, an early example of such record-keeping.

language_notes.text: "Umpire" translates Hellanodikes, the Elean judges who presided over the Olympic games.
The tale of a man turned wolf at the sacrifice to Zeus Lycæus ("wolf Zeus") belongs to Arcadian Mount Lycaeus lore.
The Eleans struck from their records the Olympiad held by the Arcadians, who had seized control of the sanctuary; hence it was "not reckoned".
The pancratium was a brutal combination of wrestling and boxing with very few restrictions.
Isagoras' seizure of the Acropolis happened c. 508 BC, when he sought Spartan help against Cleisthenes' reforms.

context_notes.text: The Pythian games were held at Delphi in honour of Apollo, and ranked among the great Greek festivals.
Victors' statues at Olympia were normally set up after the victory; Eubotas' reversal is meant to show his certainty.
Ageladas of Argos was a famous early fifth-century sculptor, said to have taught Myron, Phidias and Polycleitus.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias reveals his rationalist, skeptical narrative voice, setting the Olympic fact against what he dismisses as boastful fictions.
A man's devotion to strength ends in self-destruction when he cannot bend his bow; his pride turns to tragedy.
Pausanias breaks from listing to give a blunt personal verdict, redefining courage as distinct from madness.
The reversal from constant good fortune hints at the coming downfall, which the next sentence explains.
